title: How to Read a Morse Code Chart: 54 Entries, Spacing and Errors
description: A 54-entry Morse chart and two-way conversion on one page: spaces between letters, / between words, a Convert button; Chinese, #, %, * and [ are unsupported.
content:
The site's Morse code converter puts both directions — text to Morse code and Morse code to text — a 54-entry chart and a result box on one page. A lookup means picking a direction, filling in something, pressing “Convert”, and reading the read-only box below; it does not convert as you type, and it does not deal with rhythm or sound.

1. The short answer: a lookup takes three steps

Step one, pick a direction: #moMode defaults to “Text → Morse Code”, and the reverse option is “Morse Code → Text”. Step two, type: in the text direction use English letters, digits or symbols; in the code direction paste by the rule “a space between letters, / between words”. Step three, press “Convert”, and the result goes into the read-only “Result” box. When the conversion throws — an unsupported character or a code it cannot recognise — the result box is cleared and the status bar switches to the error style; an empty input only reports 「请输入内容」 (“Please enter input”) and does not clear the previous result.

The three panel titles are “Morse Code Converter”, “Result” and “Morse Code Table”, and the top-right corners hold “Sample”, “Clear” and “Copy”. Loading the page only draws the table — nothing is prefilled and nothing is converted — and switching the direction does not recalculate anything; you have to press “Convert” again.

ControlSelector and labelWhat it does
Direction#moMode: Text → Morse Code (default) / Morse Code → TextDecides which function “Convert” runs
Input#moInput, placeholder “Enter text or Morse code (separate letters with spaces, words with /)”Holds the text or the code
Convert#moBtnThe only entry point for a calculation
Status#moStatusSuccess or error text
Result#moOutput, placeholder “Result will appear here”, read-onlyOutputs code or text
Copy#moCopyWrites the result box verbatim to the clipboard
Sample#moSampleFills the input with SOS CLOVER
Clear#moClearEmpties input and result and hides the status bar
Table#moTableThe 54-entry chart

2. Sample, Copy and Clear: what the three buttons do

“Sample” only puts SOS CLOVER into the input; it does not convert. Press “Convert” and the result box shows ... --- ... / -.-. .-.. --- ...- . .-. — three letters of SOS, one space, six letters of CLOVER, which is exactly enough to see the “a space between letters, / between words” convention.

“Copy” reads the current value of the result box and, after the click, shows a message confirming that the text was copied to the clipboard; the clipboard matches the result box character for character, and when the result box is empty nothing is written. “Clear” empties both the input and the result box and hides the status bar, but it does not reset the direction: the next result still requires “Convert”.

The conversion runs entirely in the browser, and the 54-entry map is written into the page script, so input is never sent to a server. Morse code has no key, though, so do not treat it as ciphertext; for a string nobody can guess, use the random number generator.

3. The 54-entry chart: why 0–9 comes first

The table holds 54 entries: 26 uppercase letters, 10 digits and 18 symbols . , ? ' ! / ( ) & : ; = + - _ " $ @. The DOM order does not start at A–Z but runs 0–9, then A–Z, then the 18 symbols. The reason is that the map is a JavaScript object: integer-style keys (“0” to “9”) come before string keys when properties are enumerated, and the script draws the table straight from Object.entries.

At 1280 pixels wide it lays out as 9 columns and 6 rows: the first row runs 0 to 8, the second starts at 9, the block of letters reaches into the fourth row, and the last two rows are symbols. Each cell is two runs of text, character then code. The source gives .mo-item a flex layout, a background and a monospace font, but the entries are inserted afterwards by script through innerHTML and never receive an Astro style-scope marker, so those rules do not apply: what you see is plain block-level text with the letter tight against the code, as in “0-----” or “A.-”.

Reading the chart in that order is quicker: digits first, letters in the middle, symbols last. @ maps to .--.-., the same as “commercial at” in ITU-R M.1677-1, and / maps to -..-. — that is the slash character, not the word separator itself.

4. Text to code: uppercase first, then whitespace folded into word boundaries

encode calls toUpperCase() first, so lowercase is accepted and folded up: sos and SOS both give ... --- ..., and the output never keeps the original casing. It then splits on /\s+/ and drops empty strings, so a run of spaces, a tab or a newline all count as one word boundary; each word is split into characters and looked up, letters inside a word are joined with a single space, and words are joined with “space / space”.

Take SOS CLOVER: S is ... and O is ---, and the three letters join into ... --- ...; CLOVER is -.-. .-.. --- ...- . .-.; a / is inserted between the groups, giving ... --- ... / -.-. .-.. --- ...- . .-.. Typing SOS CLOVER with extra spaces, or with an extra newline, produces the same output.

Punctuation inside a word is mapped character by character too: Hi! gives .... .. -.-.--, @ gives .--.-., and 0/0 gives ----- -..-. -----. That / is the code for the slash character, -..-., which differs from the / used as a word separator: the first is a character inside a word, the second has a space on each side. If you need consistent case or full-width versus half-width input, run the text through the text transform tool first.

5. Code to text: / splits words, letters are not separated

decode splits on / first, trims each segment, splits it on whitespace, drops empty strings and looks every code up in the reverse map; letters inside a word are concatenated directly, and words are joined with one space. So ... --- ... gives SOS, not S O S, and .... . .-.. .-.. --- / .-- --- .-. .-.. -.. gives HELLO WORLD.

Extra slashes become extra spaces. ... / / ... splits into three segments — ..., an empty one and ... — and the three are joined with single spaces, so the result is S S with two spaces; ... // --- likewise gives S O. A leading / produces a leading space (/ ... → S) and a trailing / produces a trailing space (... / → S ), neither of which is easy to spot.

The dots in code must be ASCII full stops, not a full-width period, an interpunct or “·”: typing · reports “Unrecognized code: ·” (on the Chinese page, 「无法识别的电码：·」), and so does an ellipsis “…”. Every token must equal one entry in the table exactly; case-insensitivity exists only in the encoding direction.

Letters sticking together is not a fault: the reverse table maps one code segment to one character, and the results are concatenated. To keep letter boundaries, separate them with /, as in ... / --- / ..., which gives S O S; but then the spaces in the output are separators rather than the original word gaps.

6. Unsupported characters: what Chinese, #, %, * and [ do

The map has only 54 entries, so encoding throws as soon as it meets a character outside it, the status bar shows “Unsupported character: X (Morse code supports letters, numbers, and common symbols)” — on the Chinese page 「暂不支持字符：X」 — and the result box is cleared. X is the first unsupported character in word order: a Chinese phrase reports its first character 中, A#B reports #, and ABC， reports 「，」. Chinese text, emoji, é (which becomes É first) and full-width Ａ all take this path; the tool-list description says it supports Chinese and English, but the converter only accepts ASCII letters, digits and those 18 symbols.

# % * [ are all missing from the table. ITU-R M.1677-1 does give substitute sendings for %: percent is sent as “0 / 0”, per-mille as “0 / 00”, and the multiplication sign as the letter X. The tool implements none of that — it maps literally, so % raises the error; if you need a percent sign, type 0/0 by hand and get ----- -..-. -----.

The table also carries symbols beyond the ITU main table: ! & ; _ $ are not among the punctuation listed in M.1677-1, yet the page's 54 entries include them; &'s .-... is the same signal as the ITU “wait” prosign. The tool looks only at the characters, so the same run of dots and dashes is read as & rather than as a prosign.

7. What it does not do: sound, timing, speed and prosigns

The page has no play button, no speaker icon, no AudioContext and no oscillator, and no speed (WPM) or pitch setting; it writes dots and dashes as text and never turns them into sound. There is no waveform, timing diagram or gap check either: one space stands for a letter gap and / for a word gap, and both are writing conventions only. To see which local capabilities a browser exposes, compare the browser info detector, though that will not make this page speak either.

Under ITU-R M.1677-1 a dash is three dots long, the gap inside a letter is one dot, the gap between letters is three dots and the gap between words is seven. The tool compresses those relations into “one space” and “ / ”, which suits comparison and copying rather than sending practice. A real SOS is a prosign sent without letter gaps, while the tool outputs three letters ... --- ...; sent with letter gaps, that is not the same signal.

8. Common mistakes and a self-check list

The four most common mistakes: reading the / in the output as a slash letter; staring at an empty result box because “Convert” was never pressed; pasting Chinese punctuation or full-width letters; and typing extra slashes when decoding, which leaves invisible double spaces. Check in this order: confirm the direction, confirm the input holds only table characters plus ASCII spaces and slashes, then read the status bar.

  • Before encoding: the direction is “Text → Morse Code”, and the input has no Chinese, emoji or full-width characters.
  • After encoding: one space between letters, “space / space” between words, and never two spaces in a row.
  • Before decoding: one space between the codes of each letter and a single / between words; do not use a Chinese period for a dot.
  • After decoding: letters running together is normal; add / yourself if you want letter separation.
  • Before copying: if the result box is empty, press “Convert” first; what you copy is the raw text of the result box.
  • Before reuse: press “Clear” to empty input and result, but the direction stays as it was.

If you only want to check whether the chart has stuck, press “Sample” to generate SOS CLOVER and then split the result back into letters: ... --- ... is SOS, -.-. .-.. --- ...- . .-. is CLOVER, and the / between them is a word boundary. Getting through that split once is enough to stop confusing the letter separator with the word separator.

9. Limits and sources

The 54-entry table is a map hard-coded into the page; it does not follow ITU files and contains no accented letters, Cyrillic, Chinese or emoji. Results hold only for characters inside the table: anything outside either raises an encoding error or reports an unrecognised code when decoding. One code can also correspond to more than one written symbol (.-... is both & and the ITU wait), but in the tool's 54-entry reverse table .-... maps only to &, with no prosign concept.

The standard behind it is ITU-R M.1677-1 (10/2009, currently in force), which lists letters, digits, punctuation and @ and defines the dash length and the three gaps; for history and SOS usage, see Wikipedia's “Morse code”. The tool implements only “look each character up in the table plus space and slash separation”, with no timing, no prosigns and no substitute sending for characters that have no dedicated signal.

faqs.q: How do I convert between text and Morse code on this page?
faqs.a: Set #moMode to the direction you need — “Text → Morse Code” is the default — type into the input, and press “Convert”; the result appears in the read-only box. In the text direction, letters are separated by a single space and words by “space / space”; in the code direction, paste in the same format. Switching direction does not recompute anything, so press “Convert” again.

faqs.q: Why does Chinese input produce an unsupported-character error?
faqs.a: The map holds only 26 letters, 10 digits and 18 symbols, with no Chinese characters. Encoding looks characters up in word order and throws on the first one outside the table, with the message “Unsupported character: X (Morse code supports letters, numbers, and common symbols)”, and the result box is cleared at the same time. Typing a Chinese phrase reports its first character; A#B reports #.

faqs.q: Why does ... --- ... decode to SOS rather than S O S?
faqs.a: Decoding splits on / first, then on whitespace inside each word, and the looked-up letters are concatenated with an empty string, so the three letters merge into SOS. To get S O S with spaces, put a / between the letter codes as well: ... / --- / .... The spaces in that output are separators, not the original word gap.

faqs.q: Why are there two spaces in the decoded result?
faqs.a: Extra slashes create empty segments. ... / / ... splits into three parts, the middle one empty, and the three are joined with one space, so two spaces appear between S and S; ... // --- gives S O the same way. A leading / leaves a leading space and a trailing / a trailing space, both hard to see.

faqs.q: Can the page play Morse code as sound?
faqs.a: No. There is no play button, AudioContext, oscillator, speed or pitch setting; the page only outputs dots and dashes as text, and it has no waveform or timing check. The spaces and / in the output are writing separators and do not correspond to the ITU gaps of 1, 3 and 7 dots, so it suits comparison and copying rather than sending practice.

faqs.q: Why does the chart start with 0–9, and why do letters touch their codes?
faqs.a: The map is a JavaScript object, so integer-like keys from 0 to 9 come before string keys when properties are enumerated, and Object.entries renders them in that order: 0–9, A–Z, then the 18 symbols. The entries are inserted into the DOM afterwards, so they carry no Astro style-scope marker; the background, padding and monospace font declared for .mo-item never apply, and at 1280 wide the result is a plain 9-by-6 text grid with each letter tight against its code.

focus: The Morse tool does only 54 one-character mappings: in the text direction it uppercases first, splits on whitespace, joins letters with single spaces and words with /; in the code direction it splits on / and concatenates letters, so ... --- ... gives SOS and extra slashes leave extra spaces. Characters outside the table raise an error; there is no audio, timing, speed or prosign decoding.
